The prevention sciences graduate certificate combines skills with methods to understand how to reduce risk and promote health and healthy development.
There is an emphasis on examining social determinants of health with the aim of enhancing equity and decreasing disparities.
Additionally, this program provides intellectual development and training to a This certificate can be completed to meet requirements in the Master's of Professional Studies program, the Master's of Public Administration program, and the Master's of Public Health.
For the Master's of Professional Studies (30 credits total), students complete two certificates, and six additional credits of coursework.
The Prevention Science certificate can be the third certificate the students complete towards their degree.
The certificate could also be taken as a stand-alone certificate for any interested students.

For the Master's of Public Health (42 credits total), students complete 4 3-credit elective courses,so students could choose the four Prevention Science and Human Development courses for this in order to receive the certificate.
The HDF department began the Acc e ie rated Bachelor's to Master's in Human Development and Family Science (ABM-HDF) with Prevention Science emphasis degree program in the Fall 2026, and the four courses that are part of this certificate are required to these students.

Using evidence-based practices, applied learning, and real-world scenarios, students will be able to explore a range of issues through the lens of promoting and protecting health (e.g., social justice, family trauma, substance abuse and/or other addictions).
Therefore, the interdisciplinary nature of the program aims to foster meaningful interactions amongst students who bring expertise from a variety of health backgrounds.

PROGRAM REPORT SPECIAL SUMMER CURRICULUM COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-02B At the June 17, 2025 and July 16, 2025 meetings of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: BIS – Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies, Spring 2026 Appendix A Students coming in with 24 credits will be able to complete their degree (120 credits) with courses available in the accelerated online degree completion programs, credit for prior learning, and general education. COLLEGE OF NURSING: BS – Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S., Spring 2026 Appendix B - Accelerated online version of existing in-person RN to BS degree program. The University of Rhode Island College of Nursing’s Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S. program is dedicated to providing an education that will broaden your view of the world and create opportunities to transform healthcare in your own community. Building upon your clinical experience, the R.N. to B.S. program expands your scientific knowledge base, giving you a set of skills that allows you to integrate clinical practice, scientific inquiry and critical, creative thinking. You’ll graduate fully prepared for a whole new world of healthcare opportunities. Progression and Graduation Requirements Students are expected to achieve a C or higher in all required courses. In addition, students must maintain a minimum GPA of 2.2 to progress through and graduate from the College of Nursing.

Students who achieve less than a grade of C must repeat the course, obtaining a C grade or higher, before progressing in the nursing curriculum. Permission to retake the course will be granted on a space-available basis only. Even if successfully repeated, the initial grade remains on record as the first unsuccessful attempt. There are no further allowances for repeating a NUR course, and any subsequent NUR coursework of C- or below will result in dismissal. If the student should achieve a C- or less in two NUR courses in a single session or semester, he or she will be immediately dismissed from the College of Nursing. A total of 120 credits is required to earn a B.S. in Nursing. This includes program specific courses as well as general education requirements. R.N. to B.S. Degree - URI Online Required courses: BIO220 (3), BIO221 (1), BIO222 (3), BIO223 (1); BPS333 (3); CMB201 (4); STA220; WRT104 or WRT106 (3); as well as 18 credits of nursing courses as follows: NUR247, NUR252, NUR347, NUR441, NUR442, NUR447. A grade of C or higher is required in each of these courses. General Education. All College of Nursing Students must meet the University's General Education requirements. General education consists of 40 credits. For more details regarding General Education, please go to the Academic Requirements and Policies section of this catalog.

INFORMATIONAL MATTERS GCH101G | Topics in Civic Knowledge Newly Approved Topics for General Education Outcome C1-Full & GC In Data We Trust: Truth in Public Health This course explores how health information impacts individual health choices and public health, with an emphasis on critically evaluating data and evidence from credible sources. Students will also reflect on their civic responsibility to engage ethically and collaboratively in strengthening trust and validity in health communication. Health and Disease: Teetering on Disaster Many countries have undergone a shift from acute infectious to chronic diseases and this transformation is often fostered by changes in social norms, the economic climate, and political infrastructure, often generating issues of public importance and concern. Epidemiological methods, grounded in overarching ethical theories, provide a useful approach to evaluate these changes. This course will introduce students to relevant theories of population health and ethics, and then apply these frameworks to modern case studies. Students will gain an understanding of how social, environmental, economic, and political forces influence public health and identify opportunities and responsibilities for positively impacting the health of communities in the US and globally. This class is designed to provide students with a view of health and disease as a member of local and global community and stimulate their thinking about ways they can impact the health of their communities as a member of those communities, not necessarily as a public health professional.
